Let $S$ be any set, possibly infinite, and let $m:S\times S\to\{1,2,3,\ldots\}\cup\{\infty\}$ be a Coxeter matrix: $m(s,s)=1$, and for distinct $s,t$, $m(s,t)=m(t,s)\in\{2,3,\ldots\}\cup\{\infty\}$. Let $F(S)$ be the free group on $S$, let $N$ be the normal closure of
$$
\{s^2:s\in S\}\cup\{(st)^{m(s,t)}:s\ne t,\ m(s,t)<\infty\},
$$
and define $W=F(S)/N$. The image of $s\in S$ in $W$ is also denoted $s$. This is the Coxeter group presented by $(S,m)$.

For $w\in W$, define its length by
$$
\ell(w)=\min\{k\in\mathbb N: w=s_1\cdots s_k\text{ for some }s_1,\ldots,s_k\in S\}.
$$
The set is nonempty because every element of the quotient has a finite word in $S\cup S^{-1}$ and the relators give $s^{-1}=s$; its minimum exists by the well-ordering principle. A word of length $\ell(w)$ for $w$ is a reduced expression; the empty word is the reduced expression of $1$.

Define the reflection set $T=\{x s x^{-1}:x\in W,\ s\in S\}$. Write $u\to v$ if $v=ut$ for a reflection $t\in T$ and $\ell(v)>\ell(u)$. Define the reflection-chain Bruhat order by $u\le v$ if there is a finite chain $u=u_0\to u_1\to\cdots\to u_k=v$; the empty chain is allowed. Length strictly increases on each nonempty chain, so this relation is a partial order. The exact reduced-subword description and finite-interval consequence needed below are established in [[thm-arbitrary-rank-finite-parabolics-and-bruhat-subword]].

When $S$ is finite, the presentation and length agree with [[def-hh-coxeter-matrix-word-group-and-length]], and the reflection-chain order agrees with [[def-cg-bruhat-order-by-reflection-chains]]. No exchange, standard-parabolic, reduced-subword, or interval-finiteness property is included in this definition; those properties are justified separately.

Let $(S,m)$ be a finite Coxeter matrix with presented group $W$, length $\ell$ and geometric representation $\sigma:W\to\mathrm{GL}_K(E)$ as in [[def-hh-coxeter-matrix-word-group-and-length]], [[def-hh-geometric-coxeter-representation-and-roots]] and [[lem-hh-dihedral-root-recurrence-and-root-sign]], and let $J\subseteq S$.

1. **Support and reduction.** For every $w\in W$ the set $S(w)$ of letters occurring in a reduced expression of $w$ is independent of the reduced expression, and every word in $S$ representing $w$ can be transformed into a reduced expression by repeatedly deleting two letters (Tits reduction, using only letters already present). Consequently
$$W_J=\langle J\rangle=\{w\in W:S(w)\subseteq J\}.$$
2. **Intrinsic parabolic presentation.** Let $W_J^\ast$ be the group presented by the restricted Coxeter matrix $(J,m|_J)$ in the sense of [[def-hh-coxeter-matrix-word-group-and-length]]. The canonical homomorphism $W_J^\ast\to W_J$, $s\mapsto s$, is an isomorphism. Hence $(W_J,J)$ is a Coxeter system, its intrinsic length function $\ell_J$ agrees with the ambient length $\ell$ on $W_J$, and $W_J\cap S=J$.
3. **Minimal coset representatives.** Every right coset $W_J a:=\{ua:u\in W_J\}$ ($a\in W$, [[def-coset]]) has a unique element $d$ of minimal length; it is characterized by $\ell(sd)>\ell(d)$ for all $s\in J$, and it satisfies
$$\ell(ud)=\ell(u)+\ell(d)\qquad\text{for all }u\in W_J .$$
Equivalently, every $w\in W$ has a unique factorization $w=u\,d$ with $u\in W_J$ and $d$ the minimal representative of the right coset $W_J d$, and then $\ell(w)=\ell(u)+\ell(d)$. By inversion ($w\mapsto w^{-1}$ preserves lengths and interchanges the two coset families $\{W_Ja\}$ and $\{aW_J\}$), every left coset $aW_J:=\{au:u\in W_J\}$ has a unique minimal element $d$, characterized by $\ell(ds)>\ell(d)$ for all $s\in J$ and satisfying $\ell(du)=\ell(d)+\ell(u)$ for all $u\in W_J$.
4. **Type A.** Let $n\ge2$, $S=\{s_1,\dots,s_{n-1}\}$ and $m(s_i,s_j):=3$ if $|i-j|=1$, $m(s_i,s_j):=2$ if $|i-j|>1$ (a Coxeter matrix of type $A_{n-1}$). Then $s_i\mapsto(i\ i+1)$ extends to an isomorphism $W\to S_n$ (the letters $1,\dots,n$ carry the library's symmetric group by the order-preserving identification with $\{0,\dots,n-1\}$, under which $(i\ i+1)$ is the adjacent transposition $(i-1\ i)$), and for every $w\in W$,
$$\ell(w)=\operatorname{inv}\bigl(\varphi(w)\bigr),$$
the inversion number of the corresponding permutation ([[def-inversions-inversion-number-and-sign]]). In particular a word in the $s_i$ is reduced if and only if its length equals the inversion number of its value.

Let $(S,m)$ be a finite Coxeter matrix, $W$ the presented group, $\ell$ its length function, and let $T$, $\eta$, $\Phi$ and the right action of $W$ on $\{\pm1\}\times T$ be as in [[lem-hh-dihedral-root-recurrence-and-root-sign]].

1. **Sign character and parity.** There is a unique homomorphism $\operatorname{sgn}:W\to\{\pm1\}$ with $\operatorname{sgn}(s)=-1$ for all $s\in S$, and $\operatorname{sgn}(w)=(-1)^{\ell(w)}$ for all $w\in W$. Consequently, for all $w\in W$ and $s\in S$,
$$\ell(sw)=\ell(w)\pm1,\qquad \ell(ws)=\ell(w)\pm1,$$
with $\ell(sw)\equiv\ell(w)+1\pmod2$ and $\ell(ws)\equiv\ell(w)+1\pmod2$.
2. **Exchange.** Let $w=s_1\cdots s_k$ be a reduced expression and let $s\in S$ satisfy $\ell(sw)=k-1$. Then
$$sw=s_1\cdots\widehat{s_i}\cdots s_k$$
for some $i\in\{1,\dots,k\}$; equivalently, $w$ has a reduced expression beginning with $s$, and $s$ is a prefix reflection of any reduced expression of $w$. Right-handed form: if $\ell(ws)=k-1$ then $ws=s_1\cdots\widehat{s_i}\cdots s_k$ for some $i$.
3. **Deletion.** If the word $(s_1,\dots,s_k)$ in $S$ is not reduced, then there are $i<j$ with
$$s_1\cdots\widehat{s_i}\cdots\widehat{s_j}\cdots s_k=s_1\cdots s_k .$$
Hence repeated deletion of two letters transforms every word into a reduced expression for the same element, and a word is reduced if and only if it cannot be shortened by deleting two letters.
4. **Faithfulness of the signed action.** The right action of $W$ on $\{\pm1\}\times T$ is faithful, so $W$ embeds in $\operatorname{Sym}(\{\pm1\}\times T)$; in particular distinct simple generators are distinct in $W$.

Let $(S,m)$ be a Coxeter matrix ([[def-hh-coxeter-matrix-word-group-and-length]]), let $W$ be the presented group with length function $\ell$ and identity $1$ ([[def-hh-coxeter-matrix-word-group-and-length]]), and let
$$T=\{wsw^{-1}:w\in W,\ s\in S\}$$
be its set of reflections ([[def-cg-canonical-reflection-homomorphism]] (2)).

**(1) The Bruhat graph and the Bruhat order.** For $u,v\in W$ write $u\to v$ if $v=ut$ for some $t\in T$ with $\ell(v)>\ell(u)$. The directed graph on $W$ with these edges is the **Bruhat graph** of $(W,S)$. Define $u\le v$ if there exist $u_0,\dots,u_k\in W$ with $u=u_0\to u_1\to\cdots\to u_k=v$; the empty chain ($k=0$) is allowed, so $u\le u$ for every $u$. This relation is the **Bruhat order** on $W$. Both $\to$ and $\le$ are predicates on $W\times W$ defined from the length function of [[def-hh-coxeter-matrix-word-group-and-length]], and chains in the definition of $\le$ are finite sequences of elements of $W$, so both relations are well defined; every object below is a subset or a predicate on the fixed group $W$, and no choice principle is used anywhere in this definition.

**(2) Partial order and the identity.** $\le$ is a partial order on $W$: it is reflexive and transitive by construction (an empty chain, and concatenation of chains), and it is antisymmetric because $\ell$ strictly increases along every edge, so a chain from $u$ to $v$ containing at least one edge satisfies $\ell(u)<\ell(v)$ ([[def-natural-numbers]]). Consequently $u\le v$ together with $\ell(u)=\ell(v)$ forces $u=v$, and every $u<v$ (that is, $u\le v$ and $u\ne v$) satisfies $\ell(u)<\ell(v)$. Moreover $1\le w$ for every $w\in W$: for a reduced expression $w=s_1\cdots s_k$ and $w_j:=s_1\cdots s_j$ one has $\ell(w_j)=j$ (a shorter expression for the prefix $s_1\cdots s_j$, substituted into $s_1\cdots s_k$, would be a word of length $<k$ for $w$), so $w_{j-1}\to w_j$ because $w_{j-1}^{-1}w_j=s_j=1\cdot s_j\cdot 1^{-1}\in T$ and $\ell(w_j)=j>\ell(w_{j-1})=j-1$ ([[def-group]]).

**(3) Inversion and left multiplication.** For all $u,v\in W$ one has $u\le v$ if and only if $u^{-1}\le v^{-1}$. More precisely, a chain $u=u_0\to\cdots\to u_k=v$ with $u_{j+1}=u_jt_j$, $t_j\in T$, inverts to the chain $u^{-1}=u_0^{-1}\to\cdots\to u_k^{-1}=v^{-1}$, because
$$u_{j+1}^{-1}=t_ju_j^{-1}=u_j^{-1}\,(u_jt_ju_j^{-1})$$
with $u_jt_ju_j^{-1}\in T$ and $\ell(u_{j+1}^{-1})=\ell(u_{j+1})>\ell(u_j)=\ell(u_j^{-1})$; here $\ell(x)=\ell(x^{-1})$ holds because reversing a reduced expression of $x$ gives a reduced expression of $x^{-1}$ ([[thm-hh-parabolic-minimal-representatives-and-length-additivity]] (3)). Consequently the order is also generated by left multiplication by reflections: if $x\in W$, $t\in T$ and $\ell(tx)>\ell(x)$, then $x\to tx$, since $x^{-1}(tx)=x^{-1}tx\in T$ and $T$ is closed under conjugation ([[def-group]]).

**(4) Reflection parity.** If $x\in W$ and $t\in T$ then $\ell(xt)\equiv\ell(x)+1\pmod 2$, so $\ell(xt)\ne\ell(x)$; in particular $x\to xt$ if and only if $\ell(xt)>\ell(x)$, and for each pair $(x,t)$ exactly one of the relations $x\to xt$, $xt\to x$ holds. Indeed [[thm-hh-coxeter-exchange-deletion-and-faithfulness]] (1) supplies the sign character $\operatorname{sgn}:W\to\{\pm1\}$ with $\operatorname{sgn}(s)=-1$ for all $s\in S$ and $\operatorname{sgn}(x)=(-1)^{\ell(x)}$ for all $x\in W$; as $\operatorname{sgn}$ is a homomorphism into the abelian group $\{\pm1\}$ ([[def-group]]) one has $\operatorname{sgn}(wsw^{-1})=\operatorname{sgn}(s)=-1$ for every $w\in W$ and $s\in S$, so $\operatorname{sgn}(t)=-1$ for every $t\in T$, and then $\operatorname{sgn}(xt)=-\operatorname{sgn}(x)$ gives the asserted congruence.

The **interval** $[u,v]:=\{x\in W:u\le x\le v\}$ and the statement that $\ell$ is a rank function are introduced only after the saturated-chain results of [[lem-cg-bruhat-chain-refinement-and-gradedness]]. The subword description of $\le$ used throughout this page is the theorem [[thm-cg-bruhat-subword-characterization]], the recorded justifier of this definition; no subword assertion is made here.

Let $w\in W$ have reduced expression $w=s_1\cdots s_q$ ([[def-hh-coxeter-matrix-word-group-and-length]]) and let $\le$ be the Bruhat order ([[def-cg-bruhat-order-by-reflection-chains]]).

**(1) Subword criterion.** For every $u\in W$,
$$u\le w\iff\text{there exist }1\le i_1<\cdots<i_k\le q\text{ with }u=s_{i_1}\cdots s_{i_k},$$
and the indices may be chosen with $k=\ell(u)$, so that $s_{i_1}\cdots s_{i_k}$ is then a reduced expression of $u$.

**(2) Expression independence.** For all $u,w\in W$ the following are equivalent: (a) $u\le w$; (b) every reduced expression of $w$ has a subword that is a reduced expression of $u$; (c) some reduced expression of $w$ has a subword that is a reduced expression of $u$.

**(3) The identity.** In particular $1\le w$ for every $w\in W$: the empty subword of any reduced expression realizes the identity.

Let $S$ be any set with Coxeter matrix $m$, and let $W,\ell,T,\le$ be as in [[def-arbitrary-rank-coxeter-system-and-bruhat-order]]. For a finite $J\subseteq S$, let $W_J^*$ be the group presented by the restricted matrix $m|_J$, and let $\phi_J:W_J^*\to W$ send each generator to the same-named element.

1. The map $\phi_J$ is injective with image $\langle J\rangle$, and intrinsic length in $W_J^*$ equals ambient length in $W$ on this subgroup.
2. For $y,w\in W$, $y\le w$ if and only if a reduced expression of $y$ occurs as a subword of any fixed reduced expression of $w$. In particular, the interval $\{y:y\le w\}$ is finite and has at most $2^{\ell(w)}$ elements.
3. For every $s\in S$ and $w\in W$, $\ell(sw)=\ell(w)\pm1$ and $\ell(ws)=\ell(w)\pm1$.

Let $(S,m)$ be a finite Coxeter matrix; let $W$ and $\ell$ be the presented group and its length and let $\sigma:W\to\mathrm{GL}_K(E)$ be the geometric representation, as in [[def-hh-coxeter-matrix-word-group-and-length]], [[def-hh-geometric-coxeter-representation-and-roots]] and [[lem-hh-dihedral-root-recurrence-and-root-sign]], with reflection set $T$ and sign-change sets $\Phi(w)$ as in that lemma. Parts (1) and (2) hold for every finite $S$, including the empty and singleton cases; a distinct pair is required only for part (3).

1. **Braid moves.** Call two words in $S$ *braid-equivalent* when one is obtained from the other by finitely many replacements of an alternating subword $s\,t\,s\,t\cdots$ of length $m(s,t)<\infty$ by the alternating word $t\,s\,t\,s\cdots$ of the same length. Then any two reduced expressions of the same element $w\in W$ are braid-equivalent.
2. **M-reducedness.** A word is reduced if and only if no sequence of braid moves followed by cancellation of a consecutive equal pair can shorten it (M-reduced in the sense of [Davis, Definition 3.4.1]).
3. **Singleton detection in dihedral subgroups.** Fix distinct $s,t\in S$ and put $m:=m(s,t)$. The subgroup $\langle s,t\rangle\le W$ is dihedral of order $2m$ when $m<\infty$ and infinite dihedral when $m=\infty$; every element of $\langle s,t\rangle$ acts on the quotient $E/\operatorname{span}(\alpha_s,\alpha_t)$ as the identity, while for every $u\in S\setminus\{s,t\}$ one has $\sigma_u(\alpha_u)-\alpha_u=-2\alpha_u\notin\operatorname{span}(\alpha_s,\alpha_t)$ (no induced quotient map for $\sigma_u$ is assumed). Consequently
$$S\cap\langle s,t\rangle=\{s,t\},$$
and every element of $\langle s,t\rangle$ has a reduced expression with all letters in $\{s,t\}$ (so the alternating words of length $q\le m$, and any $q$ when $m=\infty$, are reduced in $W$).

Let $(W,S)$ be as in [[def-arbitrary-rank-coxeter-system-and-bruhat-order]]. A **totally ordered abelian group** $(\Gamma,+,0,<)$ is an abelian group with a total order invariant under translation. Its group algebra $A=\mathbb Z[\Gamma]$ consists of finite sums $\sum_{\gamma\in\Gamma}a_\gamma v^\gamma$, where $a_\gamma\in\mathbb Z$, with $v^\gamma v^\delta=v^{\gamma+\delta}$. Define the ring involution $\overline{v^\gamma}=v^{-\gamma}$, and set
$$
A_{<0}=\bigoplus_{\gamma<0}\mathbb Z v^\gamma,\qquad A_{\le0}=\bigoplus_{\gamma\le0}\mathbb Z v^\gamma.
$$

A **weight function** is a map $L:W\to\Gamma$ such that $L(xy)=L(x)+L(y)$ whenever $\ell(xy)=\ell(x)+\ell(y)$. Its simple-generator parameters are $L(s)$ for $s\in S$. The exact criterion for prescribing those values on the simple generators is proved in [[lem-simple-generator-weights-extend-to-a-weight-function]]. No sign restriction on $L(s)$ is part of this definition.

The coefficient ordering used on the weighted Kazhdan–Lusztig basis is the given order on $\Gamma$, through $A_{<0}$. The group algebra elements $v^{L(s)}$ are units for every $s\in S$.

Let $(S,m)$ be a finite Coxeter matrix, and let $K$, $E$, $(\alpha_s)_{s\in S}$, the constants $c_{st}$ and the linear maps $\sigma_s$ be as in [[def-hh-geometric-coxeter-representation-and-roots]]; let $W$ and $\ell$ be as in [[def-hh-coxeter-matrix-word-group-and-length]]. The involution, representation, signed-action and word assertions below hold for every finite $S$, including $S=\varnothing$ and $\#S=1$. Only the rank-two assertions require distinct generators.

1. **Involutions.** $\sigma_s^2=\mathrm{id}_E$ for every $s\in S$; each $\sigma_s$ is invertible, and $\ell(s)=1$.
2. **The rank-two block.** For any distinct $s,t\in S$, put $m:=m(s,t)$, $c:=c_{st}$, $P:=\operatorname{span}(\alpha_s,\alpha_t)\subseteq E$, $A:=\sigma_s\sigma_t$ and $B:=A|_P$. Then $A(P)\subseteq P$, and in the basis $(\alpha_s,\alpha_t)$,
$$B(\alpha_s)=(c^2-1)\alpha_s+c\,\alpha_t,\qquad B(\alpha_t)=-c\,\alpha_s-\alpha_t;\qquad \operatorname{tr}(B)=c^2-2,\qquad \det(B)=1 .$$
Moreover $A(v)-v\in P$ for every $v\in E$. Consequently $E=P\oplus Q$ with $Q:=\operatorname{span}\{\alpha_u:u\in S,\ u\notin\{s,t\}\}$, and for every $v=p+q$ with $p\in P$, $q\in Q$ and every $k\ge1$,
$$A^k(p+q)=B^k p+\bigl(\mathrm{id}_P+B+\cdots+B^{k-1}\bigr)\bigl(A(q)-q\bigr)+q .$$
3. **Exact order of the rank-two product.** For any distinct $s,t$ and the notation of (2), when $m<\infty$ put $\zeta:=\zeta_{st}$, of order $2m$, so $c=\zeta+\zeta^{-1}$; when $m=\infty$ use $c=2$, with no $\zeta$ stipulated. Then:
   (a) if $2<m<\infty$, the characteristic polynomial of $B$ is $X^2-(c^2-2)X+1=(X-\zeta^2)(X-\zeta^{-2})$ with distinct roots; $B$ is diagonalisable, $B^m=\mathrm{id}_P$, $\mathrm{id}_P+B+\cdots+B^{m-1}=0$, and $B^k\ne\mathrm{id}_P$ for $0<k<m$;
   (b) if $m=2$, then $c=0$ and $B=-\mathrm{id}_P$;
   (c) if $m=\infty$, then $c=2$, $B\ne\mathrm{id}_P$, $(B-\mathrm{id}_P)^2=0$, and $B^k\ne\mathrm{id}_P$ for every $k\ge1$.
   Hence $\sigma_s\sigma_t=A$ has order exactly $m$ when $m<\infty$, and infinite order when $m=\infty$; in particular $A^m=\mathrm{id}_E$ and $A^k\ne\mathrm{id}_E$ for $0<k<m$ in the finite case.
4. **The representation and the exact dihedral orders.** The assignment $s\mapsto\sigma_s$ respects every defining relator of $W$ and induces a unique homomorphism $\sigma:W\to\mathrm{GL}_K(E)$ with $\sigma(s)=\sigma_s$. Consequently, for any distinct $s,t\in S$, one has $s\ne t$ in $W$ and $st$ has order exactly $m(s,t)$ in $W$ (infinite when $m(s,t)=\infty$).
5. **The signed reflection action.** Let $T:=\{wsw^{-1}:w\in W,\ s\in S\}\subseteq W$. For $s\in S$ define $U_s:\{\pm1\}\times T\to\{\pm1\}\times T$ by
$$U_s(\varepsilon,r):=\bigl(\varepsilon\cdot(-1)^{\delta(s,r)},\ srs\bigr),$$
where $\delta(s,r)=1$ if $r=s$ and $\delta(s,r)=0$ otherwise. Then $U_s^2=\mathrm{id}$ for every $s$, and the assignment $(\varepsilon,r)\cdot s:=U_s(\varepsilon,r)$ extends to a well-defined **right action** of $W$ on $\{\pm1\}\times T$ (so $(\varepsilon,r)\cdot1=(\varepsilon,r)$ and $(\varepsilon,r)\cdot(wv)=((\varepsilon,r)\cdot w)\cdot v$). Indeed the only relations to check are $s^2=1$ and, for distinct $s,t$ with $m=m(s,t)<\infty$, $(st)^m=1$: $U_s^2=\mathrm{id}$ because for $r=s$ the two signs cancel while for $r\ne s$ one has $srs\ne s$ and $U_s(\varepsilon,srs)=(\varepsilon,r)$; and the alternating word $s\,t\,s\,t\cdots$ of length $2m$ acts trivially because its $2m$ prefix reflections $r_i:=w_{i-1}s_iw_{i-1}^{-1}$ (with $w_j:=s_1\cdots s_j$) satisfy $r_{i+m}=r_i$ for $1\le i\le m$ and $r_1,\dots,r_m$ are pairwise distinct, so each reflection of the dihedral subgroup $\langle s,t\rangle$ occurs exactly twice and every accumulated sign is even while the conjugating coordinate returns to $r$ because $(st)^m=1$.
6. **Prefix reflections, deletion and expression independence.** Let $(s_1,\dots,s_k)$ be a word in $S$ with value $w=s_1\cdots s_k$ and prefix reflections $r_i=s_1\cdots s_{i-1}s_is_{i-1}\cdots s_1$, and let $n(r):=\#\{i:r_i=r\}$.
   (a) If $r_i=r_j$ for some $i<j$, then $s_1\cdots\widehat{s_i}\cdots\widehat{s_j}\cdots s_k=w$: the two letters $s_i,s_j$ can be deleted.
   (b) $(-1)^{n(r)}=:\eta(r,w)$ depends only on $w$ and $r$, and the right action satisfies $(\varepsilon,r)\cdot w=(\varepsilon\,\eta(r,w),\,w^{-1}rw)$.
   (c) If the word is reduced ($k=\ell(w)$), then $n(r)\in\{0,1\}$ for every $r$, the map $i\mapsto r_i$ is injective, and the set $\Phi(w):=\{r_1,\dots,r_k\}=\{r\in T:\eta(r,w)=-1\}$ is independent of the reduced expression chosen, with $\#\Phi(w)=\ell(w)$.
7. **Ambient reducedness of dihedral words.** Let $s\ne t$, $m:=m(s,t)$, and for $q\ge1$ let $w_q$ be the value of the alternating word of length $q$ beginning with $s$. If $m<\infty$ and $q\le m$, or if $m=\infty$ and $q\ge1$, then $\ell(w_q)=q$, every word in $S$ representing $w_q$ has length at least $q$, and $w_1,\dots,w_q$ are pairwise distinct. Thus dihedral alternating words are reduced in the ambient group $W$, not merely inside $\langle s,t\rangle$.

Length-additive concatenation is reduced, giving additivity; every extension must equal the sum on each reduced expression.

$$I^L_{\le\mathcal C}=\operatorname{span}_A\{C_x:x\le_L y\text{ for some }y\in\mathcal C\},\qquad I^L_{<\mathcal C}=\operatorname{span}_A\{C_x:x\le_L y\text{ for some }y\in\mathcal C,\ x\notin\mathcal C\}.$$
Define $I^R_{\le\mathcal C}, I^R_{<\mathcal C}$ for a right cell and $I^{LR}_{\le\mathcal C}, I^{LR}_{<\mathcal C}$ for a two-sided cell in the same way, using the corresponding preorder. The associated left cell quotient, right cell quotient, and two-sided cell quotient are respectively $I^L_{\le\mathcal C}/I^L_{<\mathcal C}$, $I^R_{\le\mathcal C}/I^R_{<\mathcal C}$, and $I^{LR}_{\le\mathcal C}/I^{LR}_{<\mathcal C}$. [[thm-unequal-parameter-cell-quotients-are-modules]] proves that these quotients inherit the stated module or bimodule actions and have bases indexed by their cells.

For every Coxeter system and weight function of [[def-unequal-parameter-coxeter-hecke-algebra]], the spans $I^L_{\le\mathcal C}$ and $I^L_{<\mathcal C}$ attached to a left cell are left ideals; the right-cell spans are right ideals; and the two-sided-cell spans are two-sided ideals. Therefore the quotients defined in [[def-unequal-parameter-cells-and-cell-quotients]] are left modules, right modules, or bimodules, respectively. Each quotient has an $A$-basis consisting exactly of the images of the KL basis elements indexed by its cell. No further cell property, semisimplicity, or irreducible-module classification is asserted.

Let $O$ be a nonfield discrete valuation ring, equivalently a local principal ideal domain with nonzero maximal ideal ([[thm-equivalent-characterisations-of-a-dvr]]). Write $K$ for its fraction field, $\mathfrak m$ for its maximal ideal, and $k=O/\mathfrak m$ for its residue field. Let $H_O$ be a finite free $O$-algebra, so it has finite rank as an $O$-module. Assume the generic algebra $H_K=K\otimes_O H_O$ is split semisimple, meaning a finite product of full matrix algebras over $K$; assume $H_k=k\otimes_O H_O$ is split, meaning each simple module remains simple after extending the field. A simple module is a nonzero module with no proper nonzero submodule. Write $\operatorname{Irr}(H_K)$ and $\operatorname{Irr}(H_k)$ for their isomorphism classes of simple modules. For each $E\in\operatorname{Irr}(H_K)$, choose an $H_O$-stable $O$-lattice $\Lambda_E\subset E$, meaning a finite free $O$-submodule spanning $E$ over $K$. Assume each simple $M\in\operatorname{Irr}(H_k)$ occurs in at least one reduction $\Lambda_E/\mathfrak m\Lambda_E$, so every column below is nonzero. For such $M$, let
$$
d_{E,M}=[\Lambda_E/\mathfrak m\Lambda_E:M]
$$
be the multiplicity of $M$ among the composition factors of this finite-dimensional $H_k$-module. A composition series is a finite strict submodule chain with simple successive quotients; one exists by induction on module dimension, and Jordan–Hölder makes its multiplicities independent of the chosen series ([[def-composition-series-and-composition-factors-of-an-object]], [[thm-jordan-holder-theorem-in-an-abelian-category]]). The matrix $D=(d_{E,M})$ is the decomposition matrix for these chosen lattices. No general choice-independence theorem for $D$ is asserted here; in the explicit specialization below, the lattices and their reductions are given directly.

Fix an integer-valued statistic $\alpha_E$ on $\operatorname{Irr}(H_K)$. In Geck's finite-Weyl Hecke convention this is the Schur-element exponent denoted $\alpha_E$; its particular values do not enter the identity-matrix case. Put
$$
\check\alpha_M=\min\{\alpha_E:d_{E,M}>0\}.
$$
A subset $B\subseteq\operatorname{Irr}(H_K)$ is a **canonical basic set** (relative to $D$ and $\alpha$) if there is a bijection $M\mapsto E(M)$ from $\operatorname{Irr}(H_k)$ to $B$ satisfying
$$
d_{E(M),M}=1,\qquad \alpha_{E(M)}=\check\alpha_M,
$$
and, for every $E,M$,
$$
d_{E,M}>0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \check\alpha_M<\alpha_E\ \text{or}\ E=E(M).
$$
This is a definition only; it makes no claim that such a subset exists in every specialization.
